categories.definition: Gives the agent a mental model of what this repo is and where things live, so it can locate the right file or subsystem without searching or guessing.
includes: One-paragraph 'what this project is' framing, often with language/framework/version inventory
Directory trees and module maps annotated with responsibility per path
Tables mapping a task or concept to the file that owns it ('Where to Look', 'Key Files')
Descriptions of the runtime/architecture model (process roles, layers, data flow, pipeline stages)
Project-specific vocabulary defined so the agent uses the same words as the codebase
Statements of project status/maturity that set the ambient bar (e.g. 'maturing mode', 'stable/maintenance')
excludes: 'Read docs/x.md before touching y' belongs to context-routing — it defers the knowledge instead of carrying it
'Never put business logic in API handlers' belongs to protected-invariants — it constrains what you write, not what exists
Environment facts you would only learn by hitting a failure belong to pitfall-warnings
discriminators: Does the block itself carry the knowledge, or does it point at another artifact that carries it? (carry = orientation, point = context-routing)
Could a careful reader derive this by reading the repo (orientation), or only by running into a failure (pitfall-warnings)?
Is it describing what exists (orientation) or prescribing what must hold in new code (protected-invariants)?

categories.definition: Tells the agent which other document, rule file, or scoped instruction set to load, and under what condition, so the root file acts as a dispatcher rather than as the content itself.
includes: Task→guide routing tables that must be consulted before research or coding
Lists of directory-scoped AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md files with the paths they govern
'Read next' / 'read these before non-trivial changes' pointers to ADRs, principles, glossaries, lessons files
Conditional loading rules that say when NOT to load a supplemental guide
Refusal semantics attached to a pointer ('if the guide conflicts with the request, refuse')
Explicit statements that this file is a map and depth belongs elsewhere
excludes: A catalog of invocable skills/tools belongs to capability-surface — those extend what the agent can do, not what it should read
Content that is fully stated inline belongs to repo-orientation or protected-invariants
'Update docs/x.md when you change y' belongs to cochange-duties — that is a write obligation, not a read one
discriminators: Is the agent being told to READ something else (routing) or to INVOKE something else (capability-surface)?
Does the block state a condition under which the pointer fires ('when working under docs/', 'only for TS compiler API changes')? Conditional pointers are routing even when the target is a skill file.
Is the referenced artifact consumed before the work (routing) or written after it (cochange-duties)?

categories.definition: Supplies the exact invocation for building, running, testing, linting, or generating in this repo so the agent does not have to infer it from config files or invent flags.
includes: Command tables or fenced blocks for build / dev server / test / lint / format / typecheck / codegen
Package-manager-specific invocations and the wrapper script that must be used ('./run', 'e', 'make', 'fastlane')
Narrowing recipes: run one test file, one package, one pattern
Cost/speed annotations that steer which command to prefer ('fast self-verify', 'this is slow', 'don't run casually')
Environment setup and dependency-install sequences
excludes: The same command asserted as an obligation at a moment ('before committing, run X') belongs to completion-gates
Skills, subagents, and MCP tools belong to capability-surface — they act on the agent's repertoire, not the project's build
'This command silently hangs because of --watch' belongs to pitfall-warnings
discriminators: Is the command offered as a lookup for when you need it (recipe), or bound to a checkpoint like 'before commit / before done' (completion-gates)?
Does running it operate on the project's own artifacts — build, test, lint, migrate (recipe) — or does it give the agent a new ability (capability-surface)?
Is the note about how to invoke (recipe) or about a surprising failure of the invocation (pitfall-warnings)?

categories.definition: Enumerates the extra powers this repo has installed for the agent — skills, slash commands, subagents, MCP tools, browser drivers — and the triggers that should activate each one.
includes: Catalogs of skills / slash commands with a one-line 'what it does' and an invocation name
Keyword or phrase triggers that map user language onto a skill or mode
Named subagent roles and which kind of work routes to each
MCP tool descriptions with usage precedence ('use search-docs before any other approach')
Model-tier routing tables (haiku/sonnet/opus by task weight)
Purpose-built CLI verbs a project exposes specifically for agent use
excludes: Build/test/lint commands belong to command-recipes — they produce project artifacts, not agent leverage
'Use subagents liberally to keep context clean' belongs to agent-conduct — that is policy about using the surface, not the surface itself
'Read .claude/skills/x/SKILL.md before doing y' belongs to context-routing when the skill is being read rather than invoked
discriminators: Does the block enumerate available capabilities and their triggers (surface), or govern when/whether to reach for them (agent-conduct)?
Would the capability exist for a human developer with a shell (command-recipes), or only for an agent harness (capability-surface)?

categories.definition: Fixes the shape of whatever the agent writes — code, tests, commit text, slides — so the output is indistinguishable in form from what the project already contains.
includes: Naming, indentation, line length, import ordering, comment policy, type-usage rules
File and module organization rules (single-word filenames, one service file per module, size caps)
Test-authoring conventions: where tests live, which level to write at, naming, mocking philosophy, table-driven style
Commit-message grammar and PR/branch naming formats (conventional commits, imperative summary, branch prefixes)
Form rules for non-code artifacts the repo produces: blog post headers, doc types, slide typography and spacing
excludes: 'Never use `any` in a way that would break tenancy or data safety' — security/correctness constraints belong to protected-invariants
'Run the formatter before committing' belongs to completion-gates
'Every new component needs a story and a test' belongs to cochange-duties — that is about a second artifact, not the form of one
discriminators: If violated, is the result merely inconsistent with house taste (house-form), or incorrect / unsafe / data-losing (protected-invariants)?
Is the rule about the shape of the thing you write (house-form), or about a second artifact you must also touch (cochange-duties)?
Is it a property of the artifact (house-form) or a check performed on it (completion-gates)?

subcategories.gloss: docs, posts, slides written to house shape

categories.definition: States constraints whose violation produces something broken, unsafe, or unrecoverable rather than merely unidiomatic — protected paths, banned tooling, security and tenancy rules, correctness properties that must hold.
includes: Absolute prohibitions on tools or channels ('never npx', 'never npm — always pnpm', 'never bare pip')
Files and directories that must never be hand-edited (generated types, snapshots, versioned docs, build output, i18n)
Data-safety and destructive-operation rules (fail rather than lose data, atomic writes, no silent deletes)
Security, secrets, and multi-tenancy constraints (no cross-tenant reads, never commit credentials)
Correctness invariants of the domain ('crash > corrupt', 'mutations are pure', 'guid must be unique', 'assert invariants, don't hedge')
Dependency-introduction bans and version red lines
excludes: Constraints that lift once a human approves belong to human-authority — those are conditional, not absolute
Formatting or naming prohibitions belong to house-form
'This build flag OOMs, scope it' belongs to pitfall-warnings — it is a caveat, not a rule protecting an invariant
discriminators: Is the action forbidden outright (invariant), or permitted once someone approves it (human-authority)?
If violated, does something break, leak, or get lost (invariant), or does the code just look wrong (house-form)?
Is the block asserting a property that must hold in the system (invariant), or reporting a surprising fact about the environment (pitfall-warnings)?

categories.definition: Names the sibling artifacts that must be updated in the same change, so the agent's edit does not leave a derived file, index, registry, or document silently stale.
includes: 'Behavior change requires a doc update' rules, often with a change→target mapping table
Regeneration duties after a source edit (regenerate DB types after migrations, wire DI, CUE schemas, feature toggles, README index)
Hand-maintained registries that must be appended to (service registry, plugin manifest, sidebar/breadcrumb, skills array, module lists)
Bundled-artifact requirements ('a component ships with its story and its test')
Changelog / iteration-log / lessons-file entries required on completion
Mirror-sync duties across repos or doc trees
excludes: 'Never hand-edit generated types' is the inverse rule and belongs to protected-invariants
'Run the test suite before pushing' belongs to completion-gates — it checks the change rather than extending it
'Read the ADR before changing this area' belongs to context-routing
discriminators: Does the block name another artifact that must CHANGE alongside the code (co-change), or a check that must PASS on the code as it stands (completion-gates)?
Is the second artifact written by the agent (co-change), or merely read by it beforehand (context-routing)?
Is the derived file forbidden to touch (protected-invariants) or required to be refreshed (co-change)?

categories.definition: Defines what must be run and what evidence must exist before the agent may call the work done, commit, or push — converting 'seems fine' into a checkable condition.
includes: 'Before committing / before pushing / before declaring complete, run X' obligations
Pre-PR quality checklists with tick boxes
Statements that a narrower check is insufficient ('dotnet test alone may pass while the full build fails')
Evidence standards: run the command, read the output, then state the result; no claim without proof
Definitions of what does NOT count as done (stub tests, test.skip, TODO placeholders, unimplemented branches)
Fail-closed conditions that stop the work and require reporting instead of proceeding
excludes: The command itself, offered as a lookup, belongs to command-recipes
'Get explicit human approval before pushing' belongs to human-authority — the blocker is a person, not a check
The ordered method for the whole task belongs to task-procedure
discriminators: Is the blocker a check the agent can run itself (gate), or a person whose consent is required (human-authority)?
Is the command bound to a moment ('before commit') and mandatory (gate), or listed for reference (command-recipes)?
Does it define a pass/fail condition at a boundary (gate), or the sequence of steps leading there (task-procedure)?

categories.definition: Marks where the agent must stop and hand control to a person — which actions need approval, which decisions are not the agent's to make, and who remains accountable for the result.
includes: Approval gates on outward-facing or irreversible actions (push, merge, tag, publish, rebuild the database)
'Ask first' trigger lists (scope reduction, architecture change, public contract, new dependency, auth/RBAC, schema in production tables)
Steps explicitly reserved for the human ('leave the user to run these', 'AI must not edit package.json — a human runs npm install')
Accountability requirements: a human must review every line, must disclose AI assistance, remains responsible for correctness
Instructions to consult maintainers before a class of work
The inverse: explicit grants of full autonomy that waive confirmation
excludes: Absolute bans that no approval can lift belong to protected-invariants
Self-runnable checks belong to completion-gates
'Ask one focused question with 2-4 options' is about how to ask, and belongs to agent-conduct
discriminators: Can the agent unblock itself by running something (completion-gates), or only by a person saying yes (human-authority)?
Would approval ever make the action permissible? If never, it is protected-invariants.
Is the rule about whether to ask (human-authority) or about the form of the asking (agent-conduct)?

categories.definition: Prescribes the ordered method for a class of task — the sequence of steps and their order of operations — rather than any single check or command.
includes: Numbered SOPs for making a change (read context → plan → small steps → test → log → gate)

Plan-first policies and where plans are written
Domain-specific workflows: dependency upgrade, patch export, release cut, PR flow, deploy verification
Slice-sizing and branching discipline as process (small vertical slices, trunk-based, one branch per change)

excludes: A single pass/fail checkpoint belongs to completion-gates
The exact command text belongs to command-recipes
Reasoning posture that applies to every task regardless of type belongs to agent-conduct
discriminators: Does it prescribe an ORDER across multiple steps (procedure), or a condition at one boundary (completion-gates)?
Is it scoped to a class of task — bug fix, upgrade, release (procedure) — or to the agent's general disposition (agent-conduct)?

categories.definition: Pre-empts a specific known failure or misleading signal the agent would otherwise hit, so it does not burn a loop debugging something already understood or draw the wrong conclusion from a red result.
includes: Environment quirks: PATH resolution, sandbox layouts, tool binaries that resolve to the wrong version, ports that only bind on one host
Commands that behave surprisingly (test script defaults to --watch, whole-repo typecheck OOMs, slow compile in one package)
Symptom→cause→fix triplets for recurring errors, including version-incompatibility tables
Pre-existing failures explicitly declared as baseline noise, not the agent's fault
Behaviors that look like a bug but are intentional, and inline markers that must be honored
Cross-version API traps (renumbered enum values, deprecated internals)
excludes: Rules that protect an invariant belong to protected-invariants — a pitfall explains reality rather than constraining behavior
Descriptions of how the system is designed belong to repo-orientation
'Run this command' belongs to command-recipes even when a caveat is attached; the caveat sentence is the pitfall part
discriminators: Would you learn this only by hitting the failure (pitfall), or by reading the code (repo-orientation)?
Does the block explain a surprising fact about the environment (pitfall), or forbid an action to protect something (protected-invariants)?
Is the point 'this signal is misleading / already known' (pitfall), or 'this must pass before you are done' (completion-gates)?

residual.description: Blocks that do not do a job for the coding agent at all. Dominated by end-user product documentation pasted into an agent file — public API usage examples, feature marketing, threat-model prose aimed at the library's users, integration plugin lists, licensing, download stats, community links — plus repository change-history tables, and one meta oddity: prompts written to test whether the agent actually read the file. Also here: exhaustively enumerated command permutations that add no information over the first example (dozens of near-identical `npx mocha --require ts-node/register …` lines), which read as generated padding rather than instruction.
examples: javascript-obfuscator/javascript-obfuscator::CLAUDE.md — 'Copyright (C) 2016-2026 Timofei Kachalov' / 'Downloads: Widely used in production applications'
javascript-obfuscator/javascript-obfuscator::CLAUDE.md — '### What It Doesn't Protect - Determined attackers with time and tools' (aimed at library users, not the agent)
juice-shop/juice-shop::AGENTS.md — '## Verification of Agent Context ... you can use the following test prompts'
PVE-Tools/PVE-Tools-9::CLAUDE.md — '## 变更记录 (Changelog)' table of past refactors

observations: Topic and purpose come apart cleanly, and 'testing' is the sharpest case: in this packet it appears as a command lookup (grafana's `go test -run`), as a gate (postgres-ai's 'always run tests before pushing'), as an authoring convention (vllm's 'design before you write... reuse before create'), as an ordered procedure (quii's red-green-refactor loop), and as a philosophy about the agent's disposition (LibreChat's 'heavy mocking is a code smell, not a testing strategy'). Any taxonomy built on section headings would collapse five different jobs into one bucket.

The corpus openly contradicts itself on agent autonomy, and the contradictions are per-repo policy rather than drift. grafana: 'Before running `git push`, stop and get explicit human approval'; vllm: 'Pure code-agent PRs are not allowed'; carbon: a six-line 'Ask First' list — versus houbb/core-agent: '最少干扰 — 文件变更+命令执行全部自动确认，不给用户确认' (auto-confirm everything, never ask the user). Branching contradicts too: clincus 'Never commit directly to main' vs quii 'Work directly on `main` branch (no feature branches, no pull requests)'. There is no shared default the agent could fall back on.

A visible copy/generation lineage runs through the packet. The sentence 'This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository' appears verbatim in at least six unrelated repos; onevcat/Kingfisher's AGENTS.md is literally titled '# CLAUDE.md' and opens with that line; JaKooLit's AGENTS.md addresses WARP instead. Machine-authored provenance is explicit in others: `<!-- OMC:START --><!-- OMC:VERSION:4.15.7 -->`, `<laravel-boost-guidelines>` with `=== foundation rules ===` separators, and PVE-Tools crediting 'claude-init 架构师（自适应版）' in its changelog. Files are being cloned across tools and generated by installers, not only hand-written.

Awareness that the file itself costs context appears almost exclusively in agent-native repos, and correlates inversely with file size. streamlabs: 'Keep this file lean — it loads into every session'; OpenKB: 'Keep this file a short map — put depth in `docs/`'; meanwhile the largest file in the packet (45KB) spends most of its length on end-user product docs and enumerated lint/test permutations. Size in this corpus tracks lack of editing, not richness.

Context routing is the structural move that separates large/high-star repos from small ones. grafana lists four directory-scoped AGENTS.md files; carbon's root file is mostly a ~60-row task→guide router mixing `.claude/rules/*.md` docs and `.claude/skills/*/SKILL.md` skills in the same table; worktrunk delegates to per-directory CLAUDE.md in tests/, docs/, benches/, plugins/, src/commands/. Notably the routers do not distinguish 'document to read' from 'skill to invoke' — both are just 'load this when the task matches'.

One register appears only in large OSS projects that accept outside contributions: the agent is addressed as an untrusted submitter rather than a teammate. vllm opens with 'Breaching these guidelines can result in automatic banning' and specifies 'Fail-closed behavior'; juice-shop bans 'contribution farming'; RSSHub's file is 54 numbered rules that read as a maintainer's PR-review checklist retargeted at the author. Small personal repos (1–100 stars, high-follower owners) show the opposite shape — conduct, procedure, and taste, with almost no orientation, because the owner already knows the codebase.

The instruction file has become a maintained artifact with its own lifecycle rules. vllm links a guide titled 'Rules for modifying AGENTS.md or any domain-specific guide it references'; carbon ships a `create-agents-md` skill and requires updating `.ai/lessons.md` after corrections; mattpocock requires the `ask-matt` router skill be re-synced whenever a skill changes ('a router that lies'); juice-shop embeds prompts to verify an agent actually loaded the file; grafana version-stamps its file `<!-- version: 2.0.0 -->`.

Co-change duties are the most under-recognized purpose relative to how consequential they are: they encode the couplings a code-only view of the repo cannot show (regenerate DB types before typechecking, register the service in a hand-maintained file or it silently won't resolve, update DesignTokens.mdx in the same change, ship a component with its story and its test). Several files state these as the definition of 'complete' rather than as a nicety.
